We first learned to add numbers by counting the
sum explicitly. To add 5 and 7, we would draw 5
dots to represent the number 5, then draw 7 more
dots to represent the number 7, and finally count
the dots, 12, to get the answer. Imagine adding
large numbers this way, for instance 473 + 695!
Fortunately, we discovered a much faster way to add numbers.
We wrote the numbers one below the other in the Indian number
system, with the rightmost digit aligned. We then added each column
from right to left, remembering to add a carry to the left if the total was
equal to or more than 10.
11.1.1 Adding Numbers Digit by Digit
This is an example of an algorithm, a step-by-step procedure to arrive
at an answer. We describe an algorithm by writing down the steps as
precisely as possible. For instance, here is one way to describe our
addition algorithm.
Algorithm to add two numbers
1. Write the numbers one below the other in the Indian base-
ten place-value system so that the digits are aligned
from right to left.
2. Add the rightmost digits.
– If the sum is less than 10, write the sum directly
below the two digits. Set the value of carry to 0.
– If the sum is more than 10, write the units digit of
the sum directly below the two digits. Set the value
of carry to 1.
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II
3. Move to the next column of digits on the left. Add the
two digits and the current value of carry.
– If the sum is less than 10, write the sum directly
below the two digits. Set the value of carry to 0.
– If the sum is more than 10, write the units digit of
the sum directly below the two digits. Set the value
of carry to 1.
4. Repeat Step 3 until there are no more digits on the
left.
5. If the value of carry is 1, write 1 to the left of the
bottom row.
Exercise Set 11.1
1.
Add two 4-digit numbers using the steps we have written down.
Make sure you follow the steps precisely; do not perform any
action that is not explicitly mentioned. Are you able to obtain the
correct result?
2.
What happens if you add a 5-digit number to a 3-digit number. Do
our steps handle this situation correctly?
3.
Why is it important to align the columns from right to left?
4.
In Step 3, why cannot the value of carry be more than 1?
5.
What happens if we do not include the fifth step in the algorithm
above? Give examples where the algorithm will work correctly
and where it will fail to work.
There is also an important assumption in this algorithm, namely, that
we know how to add single digit numbers without counting them out.
Typically, any algorithm is built using such basic steps that we assume
we can perform directly.
The main advantage of this algorithm is that it is much faster than
counting explicitly. For instance, if we move from adding 3-digit numbers
to adding 4-digit numbers, we have 10 times as many dots to draw and
count. On the other hand, if we add the digits right to left, as in the
algorithm above, we only have to add 1 more column. Likewise, 5-digit
numbers would generate 100 times as many dots as 3-digit numbers,
but only 2 more columns to be added.
In concrete terms, suppose we can count one dot per second. To
count the dots in 33 + 27 would take a minute, to count 334 + 272 would
take about ten minutes, while 3347 + 2729 would take over one hour
and forty minutes.
On the other hand, suppose we work slowly and carefully and
take 15 seconds to add two single digit numbers with a carry. Adding
33 + 27 would take about half a minute, while 334 + 272 would take
about 45 seconds, while 3347 + 2729 would take about one minute.
Whenever we provide an algorithm, we also have to justify why
it works. Combining the dots and counting the sum is how addition is
defined. Why does adding individual digits from right to left result in
the sum of the two numbers? The key idea is that we are grouping each
number into units, tens, hundreds, … and adding each group separately.
Whenever a smaller group, say units, generates a large group of ten, we
carry over the newly formed ten to the tens group.
Think and Reflect
1.
See if you can complete the argument about grouping by units, tens,
hundreds, … to justify why the addition algorithm works.
2.
How would you modify the algorithm to add two decimal fractions?
In the rest of this chapter, we will explore the idea of an algorithm
in more detail and in some other contexts.

topics.title: Greatest Common Divisor
topics.text:
Let us look at a familiar problem: computing the greatest common
divisor (gcd) or highest common factor (hcf) of two numbers. We
have already learned different ways to solve this problem, using prime
factorisation and other methods.
How can we solve the problem from the definition of gcd? How do
we write down an algorithm for this?
The first step is to understand what is required and break down the
problem into smaller pieces that we know how to solve.
•
We want the greatest common divisor of two numbers.
•
For this, we need to first compute the divisors of both numbers
and note them down.
•
Once we have done this, we need to compare the two collections
of divisors and find the largest number that is present in both
collections.
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II
11.2.1 Computing the Divisors of a Number
Suppose we want to compute gcd(375, 825).
How do we find the divisors of 375? The divisors of a number are
just the factors of that number. Clearly any divisor, or factor, must lie
between 1 and 375. The simplest way to find the divisors is to check
each number between 1 and 375 and see if it divides 375.
We also have to keep track of the divisors of 375 so that we can
compare them with the divisors of 825. We can maintain each of these in
a sequence, or a list. How do we create the list of divisors of a number?
When we start, we do not know any divisors, so the list of divisors is
initially empty. Every time we find a new divisor, we add it at the end
of the list.
Here is how we can write down this algorithm to find the list of
divisors of any number n.
Algorithm to find the divisors of n
1. Start with an empty list-of-divisors.
2. For each number j in the sequence 1,2,3,...,n
– if j divides n, add j to the list-of-divisors.
Notice how we use names list-of-divisors and j to identify the
values that we keep track of in this algorithm. If we do not use j to
identify the number we are checking next as a possible divisor, it would
be clumsy to describe what to do each time we find a divisor.
Running through an algorithm step by step is also called executing
the algorithm. Let us execute this algorithm for a small number,
say 18. We use square brackets to denote a list of values — for instance,
[1, 4, 9, 16].
Let us see how this algorithm works for a small number, say 18.
•
Initially list-of-divisors is empty [ ].
•
1 divides 18, so we update list-of-divisors to [1].
•
2 divides 18, so we update list-of-divisors to [1, 2].
•
3 divides 18, so we update list-of-divisors to [1, 2, 3].
•
4 does not divide 18, so we leave list-of-divisors unchanged as
[1, 2, 3].
•
5 does not divide 18, so we leave list-of-divisors unchanged as
[1, 2, 3].
•
6 divides 18, so we update list-of-divisors to [1, 2, 3, 6].
•
7 and 8 do not divide 18, so we leave list-of-divisors unchanged
as [1, 2, 3, 6].
•
9 divides 18, so we update list-of-divisors to [1, 2, 3, 6, 9].
•
10, 11, 12, … , 17 do not divide 18, so we keep list-of-divisors
unchanged as [1, 2, 3, 6, 9].
•
18 divides 18, so we update list-of-divisors to [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18].
Thus, at the end of the algorithm we have divisors(18) = [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18].
Notice that the list is also in increasing order, because we checked for
divisors systematically, from 1 to 18.
What is the basic step that we assumed in this algorithm? It is that
we know how to compute when a smaller number divides a larger
number.
If we go through the steps of the algorithm, we get the following answers.
•
divisors(375) = [1, 3, 5, 15, 25, 75, 125, 375]
•
divisors(825) = [1, 3, 5, 11, 15, 25, 33, 55, 75, 165, 275, 825]
Think and Reflect
Try to execute the algorithm to compute the divisors of 15, 135, and 775.
How does the amount of work increase as the numbers grow?
11.2.2 Finding the Greatest Common Divisor
The second step in our procedure to find the gcd is to compare the lists
of divisors of the two numbers and find the largest number that appears
in both lists.
If we look through the divisiors of 375 and 825 above, we see that the
answer is 75. What if the numbers were 54000 and 81000?
•
divisors(54000) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20, 24, 25, 27,
30, 36, 40, 45, 48, 50, 54, 60, 72, 75, 80, 90, 100, 108, 120, 125, 135,
144, 150, 180, 200, 216, 225, 240, 250, 270, 300, 360, 375, 400, 432,
450, 500, 540, 600, 675, 720, 750, 900, 1000, 1080, 1125, 1200, 1350,
1500, 1800, 2000, 2160, 2250, 2700, 3000, 3375, 3600, 4500, 5400,
6000, 6750, 9000, 10800, 13500, 18000, 27000, 54000]
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II
•
divisors(81000) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 25,
27, 30, 36, 40, 45, 50, 54, 60, 72, 75, 81, 90, 100, 108, 120, 125,
135, 150, 162, 180, 200, 216, 225, 250, 270, 300, 324, 360, 375,
405, 450, 500, 540, 600, 648, 675, 750, 810, 900, 1000, 1080, 1125,
1350, 1500, 1620, 1800, 2025, 2250, 2700, 3000, 3240, 3375, 4050,
4500, 5400, 6750, 8100, 9000, 10125, 13500, 16200, 20250, 27000,
40500, 81000]
It is no longer so simple to just inspect the lists to find the largest
element common to both of them! We need to do this systematically.
We compute a new list, the list of common divisors. As before,
when we compute the list of divisors, this list is initially empty. For
each divisor in the first list, we check if it belongs to the second list. If
it does, we add it to the list of common divisors. Notice that 1 divides
every number, so the list of common divisors will have at least one
entry, 1.
Using this, we can compute the list of common divisors of 54000
and 81000, to be [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 25, 27, 30, 36,
40, 45, 50, 54, 60, 72, 75, 90, 100, 108, 120, 125, 135, 150, 180, 200,
216, 225, 250, 270, 300, 360, 375, 450, 500, 540, 600, 675, 750, 900,
1000, 1080, 1125, 1350, 1500, 1800, 2250, 2700, 3000, 3375, 4500, 5400,
6750, 9000, 13500, 27000].
Since we know that each list of divisors is in increasing order, it must
be the case that the list of common divisors is also in increasing order.
Hence the largest common divisor is the rightmost element in the list. In
other words the gcd of 54000 and 81000 is 27000.
11.2.3 First Algorithm for gcd
Combining the steps above, we can write out a complete algorithm to
compute the gcd of two numbers m and n. This makes use of the earlier
algorithm to compute the list of divisors of a number.
Algorithm to find gcd(m, n)
1. Let divisors-of-m be the list obtained by computing
divisors(m)
2. Let divisors-of-n be the list obtained by computing
divisors(n)
3. Start with an empty list common-divisors
4. For each number x in the list of divisors-of-m
- If x also appears in the list of divisors-of-n,add
x to the list common-divisors
5. Report the rightmost element of the list common-
divisors as gcd(m,n)
When we execute this algorithm for gcd(375, 825) we check whether
each of the divisors [1, 3, 5, 15, 25, 75, 125, 375] of 375 appears in the list
of divisors [1, 3, 5, 11, 15, 25, 33, 55, 75, 165, 275, 825] of 825. We see that
1, 3, 5, 15, 25 and 75 are in the second list while 125 and 375 are not. So
we compute the list of common divisors to be [1, 3, 5, 15, 25, 75]. Since
75 is the rightmost element in this list, gcd(375, 825) = 75.

topics.title: Data Structures
topics.text:
When we execute an algorithm, we compute intermediate quantities,
such as the list divisors-of-m and the list divisors-of-n. To keep track
of these values, we use names such as divisors-of-m and divisors-
of-n, respectively, so that we can refer to them later in the algorithm.
As we remarked earlier, assigning names to intermediate values is
important for writing down algorithms concisely.
Also, these intermediate values are typically more complicated than
just simple numbers. In this case, we maintain lists of numbers and, in
fact, lists that are arranged in ascending order. A list is an example of
a data structure. Data structures allow us to organise information in
a manner that helps make an algorithm more efficient. We will explore
this idea in higher grades.
Exercise Set 11.2
1.
Suppose List 1 and List 2 are two lists of numbers in increasing
order.
(i) Write an algorithm to find elements in List 1 that are not
present in List 2.
(ii) Write an algorithm to find elements in List 2 that are not
present in List 1.
2.
Describe an algorithm to compute the least common multiple
(lcm) of two numbers.
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II
*3.
Divisors occur in pairs. For instance, the divisors of 18 are (1, 18),
(2, 9) and (3, 6).
(i) If we write out divisors in pairs, how many numbers do we
have to examine between 1 and n to find all the divisors of n?
(ii) If we list out the divisors in pairs, will our gcd algorithm still
work in the manner we have described?
11.3.1 Improving the Algorithm
Compute both lists of divisors together
In the algorithm above, we first check all numbers between 1 and m to
find the divisors of m. Then we start again with 1 and check all numbers
between 1 and n to find the divisors of n. This means we have to scan
m + n possible divisors.
We can combine these two scans into one. Let max(m, n) be the
maximum of m and n. We run through each j from 1 to max(m, n).
•
If j divides m we add j to the list of divisors of m.
•
If j divides n we add j to the list of divisors of n.
This reduces the number of possible divisors to be checked from
m + n to max(m, n).
Directly compute the list of common divisors
If we combine the scans, we can directly compute the list of common
divisors, instead of first computing the divisors of each number and
then combining the lists.
•
For each number j from 1 to max(m, n), if j divides both m and
n, add j to the list of common divisors.
In fact, a common divisor cannot be larger than the smaller of the
two numbers, so we can check for common divisors up to the minimum
of m and n rather than the maximum.
•
For each number j from 1 to min(m, n), if j divides both m and
n, add j to the list of common divisors.
Do away with lists
Do we need to maintain the list of all common divisors? Each time
we find a larger common divisor, the ones that we have found earlier
are useless!
Example: Let m = 6, n = 12.
– min(6, 12) = 6
– Initially set most-recent-common-divisor to 1
– k = 2 divides both 6 and 12.
Update: most-recent-common-divisor to 2.
– k = 3 divides both 6 and 12.
Let us keep track of a quantity
called most-recent-common-divisor.
We know that 1 is always a
common divisor, so we can start
with most-recent-common-divisor
set to 1. We then scan all numbers
from 2 to min(m, n).
Update: most-recent-common-divisor to 3.
– k = 4 doesnot divide 6.
most-recent-common-divisor remains 3.
– k = 5 doesnot divide 6.
most-recent-common-divisor remains 3.
– k = 6 divides both 6 and 12.
Update: most-recent-common-divisor to 6.
•
For each k from 2 to
min(m, n), if k divides
both m and n, update
most-recent-common-divisor
to k.
Scan complete. gcd(6, 12) = 6
At the end of this scan,
most-recent-common-divisor directly gives us the gcd.
Exercise Set 11.3
1.
How would our original algorithm change if we computed the
divisors of n by examining the numbers from 1 to n in reverse
order, from n down to 1?
2.
What about the last algorithm described above? What happens
when we look at common divisors starting from min(m, n) and
work backwards to 1?
11.3.2 Analysing these Algorithms
We started with a very basic algorithm. Since this was derived directly
from the definition of gcd, it is easy to justify that the result it computes
is actually the gcd.
Each successive refinement that we have proposed improves the
efficiency but does not substantially change what is being computed.
Hence, we can argue that all of the algorithms we have seen so far
compute the correct value.
How efficient are these algorithms? Even in the final version, where
we eliminated lists, we had to examine all numbers from 1 to min(m, n).
This is similar to what we saw when adding numbers by counting.
If the smaller number goes from 3 digits to 4 digits, we have to scan 10
times as many values to find the common divisors. If we go from 3 digits to
5 digits, the work grows by a factor of 100.
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II
As we did for adding, can we find an algorithm for gcd where the
effort is proportional to the number of digits in the number, rather than
the value of the number?
11.3.3 Euclid’s Subtraction Algorithm
An elegant solution to achieve this was written down by Euclid, in his
book Elements. Historians believe that other Greek mathematicians
knew of this algorithm before Euclid, but he was the first to put it down
in writing.
Reducing a problem to a simpler one
The original version of Euclid’s algorithm makes use of the following
observation. Let us assume that m ≥ n. Then, gcd(m, n) is the same as
gcd(n, m – n).
Why is this the case?
•
Let d be a common divisor of m and n. Then we can write m as ad
and n as bd, where a and b are natural numbers. This means that
m – n = ad – bd = (a – b)d, so d is also a divisor of m – n.
•
On the other hand, if d divides both n and m – n, then n = xd and
m – n = yd for some natural numbers x and y. This means that
n + (m – n) = m = xd + yd = (x + y)d, so d also divides m.
This is shown visually below. If we can ‘tile’ m and n using blocks of
size d, we can also tile m – n by blocks of the same size. In fact, Euclid
used a similar pictorial proof to justify his algorithm.

Fig. 11.1: Justification for Euclid’s gcd algorithm
This observation tells us that any common divisor of m and n is also
a common divisor of n and m – n, and the converse is also true. Hence
the set of common divisors are the same in both cases, which means
that gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m – n).
Euclid’s algorithm reduces the problem of finding gcd(m, n) to that
of finding gcd(n, m – n). The second problem involves smaller numbers,
so it should be a simpler problem to solve.
How do we solve it? We apply the same strategy: reduce it to
gcd(x, y) where x = min(n, m – n) and y is the difference between n and
m – n.
When do we stop? Suppose we compute the gcd of a number with
itself, say gcd(23, 23). The answer should clearly be 23. When we
reduce this we get gcd(23, 0). In other words, if we reach gcd(m, 0), the
answer is m.
Euclid’s algorithm for gcd(m,n)
1. If m < n, reverse the numbers and compute gcd(n,m)
2. If n = 0, report the answer as m
3. Otherwise, reduce the problem to compute gcd(n,m-n)
Let us apply this algorithm to gcd(375, 825), the problem that we saw
before.
•
Since 375 < 825, Step 1 asks us to reverse the numbers and compute
gcd(825, 375).
•
Since 825 – 375 = 450, Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to
computing gcd(375, 450).
•
Since 375 < 450, Step 1 asks us to reverse the numbers and compute
gcd(450, 375).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(375, 75).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(75, 300).
•
Since 75 < 300, Step 1 asks us to reverse the numbers and compute
gcd(300, 75).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(75, 225).
•
Since 75 < 225, Step 1 asks us to reverse the numbers and compute
gcd(225, 75).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(75, 150).
•
Since 75 < 150, Step 1 asks us to reverse the numbers and compute
gcd(150, 75).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(75, 75).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(75, 0).
•
Since n = 0, Step 2 tells us the answer is 75.
In the example above, we reduced the problem 7 times before finding the
answer. Are we close to our original goal of finding an algorithm where
the effort is proportional to the number of digits? Unfortunately, no.
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II
Consider gcd(99, 2). This will reduce successively to gcd(97, 2),
gcd(95, 2), gcd(93, 2), … , gcd(5, 2), gcd(3, 2), gcd(2, 1), gcd(1, 1), and
gcd(1, 0) eventually giving us the answer 1. In general, if we start with
an odd number 2k + 1, gcd(2k + 1, 2) will require about k reductions
before we get the answer 1. This means the number of steps is
proportional to the value we start with, rather than the number of
digits used to write down the value.
11.3.4 Āryabhaṭa’s Division Algorithm
In Indian treatises like Āryabhaṭa’s Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE), we see
the “long division” method for finding GCD using Indian place value
numerals. It makes an efficient use of repeated “division by remainder”
in place of repeated subtraction. For example, when one starts with 99
and subtracts 2 repeatedly, what remains, once one cannot subtract 2
anymore, is the remainder when 99 is divided by 2.
Hence, to improve the performance of Euclid’s algorithm, we can
change the reduction step: instead of reducing gcd(m, n) to gcd(n, m – n),
we reduce it to gcd(n, m mod n), where m mod n stands for the remainder
when m is divided by n. For example, 17 mod 5 is 2 and 33 mod 7 is 5.
We saw earlier that a divisor d ‘tiles’ both m and n if and only if it
‘tiles’ both n and m – n. In a similar way, we can argue that d ‘tiles’ m and
n if and only if it tiles m and m mod n. This justifies reducing gcd(m, n) to
gcd(n, m mod n).
Here is the modified algorithm. Notice that the only change is in the
third statement. The stopping condition is the same as before.
1. If m < n, reverse the numbers and compute gcd(n,m)
2. If n = 0, report the answer as m
3. Otherwise, reduce the problem to computing gcd(n, m mod n)
Consider the earlier example gcd(99, 2) that took a long time to
converge. Here is what happens when we execute the improved
algorithm.
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(2, 1).
•
Step 3 asks us to reduce the problem to computing gcd(1, 0).
•
Since n = 0, Step 2 tells us the answer is 1.
In other words, we needed only two reduction steps to get to the
final answer. Check that this would happen for any similar problem of
the form gcd(2k + 1, 2).
The above modified algorithm can be carried out concisely using
the “long division” method given by Indians at least from the time of
Āryabhaṭa. We illustrate the method through the following examples—

In fact, it can be shown that the number of reductions needed in

involved to present here, but you will learn about it in future grades.
A Pinch of History
The influential Persian mathematician Al-Khwārizmī (780–850 CE), a
scholar at the “House of Wisdom” in Baghdad, developed a great liking
for Indian mathematics. He learnt Sanskrit, and around 820 CE wrote a
detailed treatise expounding the Indian place value number system and
the Indian procedures for the four fundamental operations — addition,
subtraction, multiplication, and division. His original is lost, but its
12th-century Latin translation, Liber Algorismi de numero Indorum
(“The Book of Al-Khwārizmī on Indian Numerals”), survives and played
a major role in spreading Indian arithmetic through medieval Europe.
Al-Khwārizmī’s name became so closely tied to these methods that the
word algorismus — from Algoritmi, the Latin form of his name — came to
mean any Indian method for numerical computation; it later contracted
to algorism and then algorithm. Etymologically, then, “algorithm”
originally denoted an Indian method of arithmetic, before it broadened
to mean any well-defined, step-by-step systematic procedure for solving
a class of problems.
Ganita Manjari | Grade 9 | Part II

Chapter Summary
• An algorithm is a systematic procedure to solve a problem.
• Algorithms consist of basic steps that we know how to execute.
• We may execute the same step a number of times; for instance, for
each j in 1, 2, ..., n, check if j is a divisor of n.
• A step in an algorithm may be conditional; for instance, add j to
the list of divisors of n only if j divides n.
• When we describe an algorithm to solve a problem, we need to
justify that it is correct.
